title: ICMR survey records lower anaemia prevalence across India

contentHtml:
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has released key findings from the Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023-2025, providing comprehensive national evidence on anaemia and micronutrient deficiencies across the life course.

SAMPADA represents one of the largest and most comprehensive nutrition surveys undertaken globally. The survey covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories. More than 1.7 lakh blood samples were analysed for haemoglobin estimation across different age, sex and physiological groups.

A major strength of SAMPADA is the use of gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation, providing greater accuracy and reproducibility. In a sub-sample, the survey also assessed iron status, folate, vitamin B12, together with inflammatory biomarkers C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) to obtain national level prevalence estimates.

The SAMPADA findings show an encouraging shift with overall lower prevalence of anaemia compared to previous surveys. The difference is particularly large in case of  children aged 12-59 months who had 42 per cent anaemia prevalence. Adolescent girls aged 10-19 years had anaemia prevalence of 46 per cent, adolescent boys aged 10-19 years and men aged 20–59 years had 22-23 per cent anaemia prevalence whereas women of reproductive age had 56 per cent prevalence.

The survey also provides nationally representative estimates among older adults, extending the assessment of anaemia to an age group for which national-level evidence has been limited. The findings also highlight important differences by age, sex, physiological status and location, reinforcing the need for population-specific approaches rather than a single strategy for all groups.

The key highlights of the report are:

Majority of anaemia is mild, highlighting opportunities for early action. Mild anaemia constitutes a substantial proportion of the overall anaemia burden. About half of anaemic women including pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls and children, have mild anaemia indicating considerably lower risk of serious health consequences than moderate or severe anaemia. Anaemia prevalence is much lower among adolescent boys, adult and older men and even among those affected, three-fourths have only mild anaemia.

Severe anaemia was observed in less than 2 per cent people in majority of the age groups.

Iron deficiency accounts for about half of the anaemia cases in women, adolescent girls and children. The micronutrient assessment shows that although iron deficiency is the predominant contributor to anaemia in vulnerable population groups, it accounts for about half of the overall anaemia burden highlighting the need to simultaneously address multiple nutritional and non-nutritional causes of anaemia including infections, hemoglobinopathies, as well as inflammation related to chronic disease. However, the prevalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency was similar in both anaemic and non-anaemic individuals across population groups, indicating limited contribution of these micronutrient deficiencies to anaemia in India.

Iron deficiency is concentrated in specific life-stages and in moderate and severe cases of anaemia. SAMPADA findings show that iron deficiency is largely restricted to population groups including under five children, adolescent girls and women of reproductive age while adolescent boys, men and the elderly have low prevalence of iron deficiency. Importantly, people with moderate and severe anaemia have a high prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified by testing for appropriate treatment and tracking till resolution as envisaged in AMB 2.0

“SAMPADA provides nationally representative estimates of anaemia across children, adolescents, adults, pregnant and lactating women and older adults, together with detailed information on micronutrient deficiencies to evaluate potential causes of anaemia. It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat”, said Dr Rajiv Bahl, Secretary, Department of Health Research, Govt of India and DG, ICMR

“These findings support more targeted, population-specific and life-course approaches to anaemia prevention and management. The evidence can contribute, while also identifying areas where further research and improved surveillance are required” explained Dr Bharati Kulkarni, Director, ICMR-NIN
